newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Jailers demand training to stop Aboriginal deaths.
newsitem.headline: Jailers demand training to stop Aboriginal deaths.

text.p: Australian prison officers said on Friday they desperately needed improved training if the number of Aboriginal deaths in jail was to be lowered.

On the eve of a national summit into Aboriginal deaths in custody, the main public sector union released a report recommending the government provide a further A$510 million (US$383 million) over the next three years to fund improvements in the prison system.
Although Aborigines amd Torres Strait Islanders make up less than two percent of Australia's 18 million people, they account for some 20 percent of deaths in custody or during arrests.

The National Prison Officers' Association said in its submission to the report, compiled by the Community and Public Sector Union, that improved training was crucial if officers were to identify potentially suicidal Aboriginal prisoners.
Association president John Dixon said many prison officers were not receiving coaching in risk assessment and crisis intervention and were missing the warning signals as a result.
"In some states they just shrug their shoulders and say their shift is about to end, but in other states alarm bells do start ringing," Dixon told a news conference.
He called for the establishment of a national body to monitor the implementation of the recommendations that arose from a 1991 official inquiry into Aboriginal deaths in custody.
Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron said the reduction of indigenous deaths in custody and high incarceration rates were priority issues that could not be ignored.

He said Friday's meeting of federal and state ministers and Aboriginal leaders would consider options developed by Aboriginal groups and look at procedures that were effectively being used in some states.
"Simply throwing money at the problem has not worked," Herron said in a statement. "We are committed to developing practical, commonsense solutions to this tragic problem."

A government report released earlier this year said Aboriginal deaths in custody had jumped to record levels as governments failed to implement measures aimed at preventing such deaths, such as using non-custodial punishments for indigenous people used to living outdoors.

In the year to end-June 1996, 19 of the 75 people who did in police custody or in prison were Aboriginal. Six of those deaths were suicides, five resulted from illness and eight stemmed from injuries sustained during or after arrest -- mostly in road accidents during police pursuits.
